terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation; the full phrase is vī ēlectricā replēre
evidence: Cic. Prov. Cons. 2.4: exhaustās domōs (sc. replēre; Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Our choice: no reference work gives a Latin verb for charging a battery. Classically replēre is to fill again what has been emptied, and Cicero pairs it with exhaustus, which gives the rest of the vocabulary: exhaustus, flat or dead; plēnus, fully charged. The meaning is plain at first hearing.
The figure the modern languages use (French charger, Italian caricare, German laden), so it will be understood; but in Latin it suggests a burden laid on something, not a store filled up.

phrases.latin: Accumulātrum paene exhaustum est; tēlephōnum replē.
phrases.english: The battery’s nearly flat; charge your phone.

phrases.latin: Accumulātrum jam dēficit; ubi est replētrum?
phrases.english: The battery’s running low; where’s the charger?

phrases.latin: Tēlephōnum exstīnctum est: accumulātrum exhaustum est.
phrases.english: The phone’s dead: the battery’s flat.
Plug the car into the charger; it’ll charge overnight.

sources: Lewis & Short: repleo · Lewis & Short: onero · Lewis & Short: exhaurio · Lewis & Short: deficio
David Morgan and Patrick Owens, Adumbratio Lexici Anglico-Latini, s.v. battery; its heading “charge, recharge (battery, cell phone, etc.)” gives no Latin.
